A Study Visit to Arignar Anna Zoological Park, Vandalur

Notes from a four-hour walk through one of India’s largest zoological parks, on animal care, careful observation and conservation.

DK
Dharaneeswaran KAuthor
24 September 2026Date of visit
8 min readReading time
Key takeaways
  • A zoo must provide food, water, shade and space for each species, so every enclosure is arranged differently.
  • Animals follow their own routines, and their welfare matters more than being visible at every moment.
  • Quiet, careful visitors help animals stay relaxed, and conservation in the wild remains equally important.

Introduction

On 24 September 2026, I visited the Arignar Anna Zoological Park at Vandalur, Chennai, together with my classmates. The park has been open to the public at its present site since 1985 and covers more than 1,400 acres, which makes it one of the largest zoological parks in India. We travelled together by bus, bought entry tickets priced at ₹200, and stayed inside for nearly four hours. This blog describes what I observed during the visit and what I took away from it.

The Layout of the Park

The park is arranged along paved footpaths, and most of them run under trees, so the walk stays shaded for a large part of the way. One stretch is a covered walkway built from a steel frame and wire mesh, with creepers growing over it. The size of the place became clear quickly. Four hours were not enough to see every enclosure, and we had to decide as a group which sections to spend time in.

Mammals

The first large animal we saw was an Asian elephant, grazing alone in a wide enclosure. The enclosure had trees, patches of bare soil and a tyre hanging from a branch, which I took to be a simple form of enrichment. The elephant paid little attention to the visitors and kept feeding.

Further along, a spotted deer (chital) was standing close to the footpath. It kept its head down and sniffed at a stone while we watched from a few metres away. The white spots on its brown coat were clearly visible, and its calm behaviour allowed everyone in the group to observe it closely.

A herd of Indian gaur was resting together under a thatched shelter. A signboard in Tamil at the fence gave the name of the species along with a short description. Most of the animals were lying down in the shade and moved very little.

The tiger enclosure was fenced with wire mesh and had tall wooden posts standing in the grass. The tiger was lying on the ground and did not move while we were there. Its stripes broke up its outline against the grass and the shadows, which showed how well the pattern works as camouflage.

Reptiles

In the reptile section, a caiman was lying at the edge of a pond with its mouth slightly open. Crocodilians often rest this way while basking in the sun, and it is thought to help them control their body temperature. The animal stayed still for as long as we stood there.

Birds

The bird enclosure had a large pond with painted storks standing in the shallow water and pelicans resting on the stones near the edge. The storks were wading slowly and feeding, while the pelicans stayed mostly on the bank. At one point a pelican opened its wings and splashed in the water, possibly while bathing.

Aquatic Life and Nocturnal Birds

The visit also included indoor displays that gave us a closer view of aquatic species and birds. These enclosures were different from the larger outdoor habitats because the glass panels allowed us to notice details such as colour, movement and feeding behaviour without standing close to the animals.

Three owls were perched together on a branch in a dim enclosure. They remained almost motionless, but their upright posture and forward-facing eyes were easy to observe. The low light and rocky background also made the enclosure feel suited to birds that are active mainly at night.

One aquarium contained an oscar fish moving slowly through plants and stones. Its dark body was marked with bright orange patches, which stood out under the aquarium lighting. Watching it swim through the water made the display feel more active than the enclosures where animals were resting.

Another tank had an albino catfish close to the glass. Its pale colour, broad fins and long barbels were clearly visible from the front. The close view helped me notice features that are easy to miss when fish are seen only from the side or at a distance.

Learning From the Visit

The visit helped me understand that a zoo is not simply a place where animals are kept for visitors to see. Each enclosure has to provide food, water, shade and enough space for the animal to rest or move around. The arrangements were different for every species. The elephant had a large open enclosure, the birds had a pond, and the aquatic animals were kept in tanks where the lighting and water conditions could be controlled. Seeing these differences made the role of daily animal care easier to understand.

I also noticed that the animals did not behave in the same way throughout the day. Some were feeding, some were resting in the shade and others stayed at a distance from the visitors. This was a useful reminder that animals in a zoological park still follow their own routines. Visitors may hope to see an animal standing close to the fence, but the welfare of the animal is more important than making it visible at every moment.

Indoor Displays and Observation

The indoor bird and aquarium displays added a different kind of experience to the visit. The glass panels made it possible to observe small details without creating noise near the animals. In the owl enclosure, the group could see the birds resting on the branch and compare their shape and markings. In the aquariums, it was possible to watch how the fish moved through plants, stones and open water. These displays encouraged us to slow down and look carefully instead of moving quickly from one enclosure to the next.

The fish photographs also showed how varied aquatic life can be. The oscar fish had a dark body with orange markings, while the albino catfish had a pale colour and long barbels near its mouth. Although both animals were in aquariums, their appearance and way of moving were very different. This made the section feel educational as well as interesting, because we could connect visible features with what we have learned about adaptation and habitat.

Visitor Responsibility and Conservation

A major lesson from the visit was that visitors have a responsibility to behave quietly and follow the park rules. Crowding near the fence, shouting or trying to attract an animal can disturb it. The signs asking people not to feed the animals are important because food brought from outside may not be suitable for them. Our group tried to keep a reasonable distance from the enclosures and spent time reading the information boards where they were available.

The park can also help visitors think about conservation. Many people know animals from textbooks, videos or social media, but seeing them directly makes their size, behaviour and habitat needs more real. At the same time, the visit showed why forests, wetlands and other natural habitats must be protected. A well-planned zoo can support education, but protecting wildlife in its natural environment remains equally important.

By the end of the four hours, our group had covered only part of the park, yet the visit had given us many things to discuss. The elephants, deer, gaur, tiger, birds, owls and fish each showed a different aspect of animal life. I came away with a stronger appreciation for careful observation and with a better understanding of why animal care, visitor discipline and conservation awareness all matter in a zoological park.

Tips for visitors

  • Wear comfortable footwear
  • Carry drinking water
  • Do not feed the animals
  • Keep quiet and keep a reasonable distance
  • Read the information boards
  • Plan which sections to see; one day is not enough

Observations

Several enclosures had been planned to resemble the animals’ natural surroundings, with trees, shelters and water. Some animals, however, stayed far from the fence, and it was not always easy to see them. The signboards were useful, but they were not available at every enclosure. It was also noticeable that the behaviour of visitors affected the animals. In quieter areas the animals were relaxed, and the park depends on visitors not feeding or disturbing them.

Conclusion

The visit gave me a better idea of how a zoological park works. Apart from displaying animals, a zoo supports conservation and gives students a chance to learn about wildlife by seeing it directly. Observing the animals at close range was different from reading about them, and I would recommend such visits to other students. For anyone planning one, comfortable footwear and drinking water are necessary, and the animals should not be fed.

Location and Getting There

Vandalur, south-west of Chennai

Arignar Anna Zoological Park
Vandalur, Chennai, Tamil Nadu 600 048

About 32 km from the city centre. Vandalur railway station is roughly 1 km from the main entrance, and city buses serve the area. We reached the park by bus.
